analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 430, James Sailors et al. versus the Board of Education of the County of Kent et al. Mr. Strawhacker, or Mr. Miles first. Yes, Mr. Chief Justice. It is the contention of the appellant, Mr. James Sailors and others, individual plaintiffs in this case, that the constitutional principle of Reynolds v. Sims and companion cases related thereto. It extends to the county level of government. And on that basis, and consistent with those decisions, any logic and in sound policy, that the equal protection clause extends no less to the local level than it does to the state level. The city of Grand Rapids, which also comprises the Grand Rapids School District, has a population of 201,000. Of those 363,000, or some 55 percent. That after World War II, as in all communities, large communities, the flight to suburbine, the core cities, became surrounded with the young, affluent populations, who generally and before that time had been living in the city to help solve the city's problems. And the city itself became the receptacle for large numbers of poorer, culturally deprived people. It is the contention of the plaintiff that in order to preserve its tax base, the plaintiff, as a citizen of the school district, the city of Grand Rapids, and others within that school district, made various annexations surrounding. And this gives rise to the particular controversy involved. Now, there's a peculiar system set up as an extension of state government into the county level. Part of county government is taken care of by a board of supervisors that handle the ditches, the roads, and matters of that type. And another part of state government delegated to the county level provides for a county board of education. Well, this is an all-powerful, important body. In the state of Michigan, under the appropriate acts, this board is composed of five people, the county board, in each of the counties of the state. Five members. Five members. And each two years, by empty. Notice goes out to each of the school districts in the county, the individual school districts in the county, of which, at the time of the origin of this case, there was some 40 to 50, to come at a common place, and each representative of each of these school districts may then cast its ballot, his ballot, for a member or two members, with the exception of the third time around, of the county board. And as the popular vote ends with the election of the local school district. The popular vote as such, Your Honor, Mr. Justice Douglas, is so set that the individual voter elector has voted for his candidates for the local school board. That local school board sends its member to this constituent assembly, which in turn elects the five members to the county board. It's a dazzle. Mr. Justice Douglas. Does that first board have proportional representation? Is the first board, Mr. Chief Justice, is elected at large in each case it has proportionate representation. At large in the county? At large within its school district. In the school districts. For instance, as a resident of the city of Grand Rapids, with some 201,000 other people, I am allowed to vote for the nine members of my school district. And that 201,000 people school district, representing 55% of the population of the whole county, is allowed one vote as it casts its vote for a member of the county board. If I was a member of an area known as Nelson Center, I would be coming from an area of 100 people. I would be casting my vote for the school board, which reflects my view, my thought, at the next county school board election. And, as a person from Nelson Center, my vote is cast for a member of the county school board equally to and alongside of that member of the city of Grand Rapids School District that has 201,000 people. Thus, we have asserted that the ratio of imbalance and the county school board for the county camp, now known as the intermediate school board, was at the time of the election of the people that took action in this case, some 2,000 to 1,000. Between the Grand Rapids School District and Nelson Center. That has now been corrected all the way to 901, as we understand. We say that there is still a hopeless imbalance. Now, the state of Michigan has delegated educational functions on the county level, and these are extremely important to every person in the county. The county board, stripped down of all of its labels, is a legislative body. It sets policy for the entire county. It has the power to tax. It has the power to levy taxes on everybody in the county. And, at the time of the creation, or voting for the constituent board that existed at the time of the action in this case, 2% of the people in Kent County could control the county board which would determine what taxes would be laid upon all of the people of the county for various functions. Special education, special education, bonding. Furthermore, the county board is empowered to set up a separate school for juvenile delinquents working with the courts. It's a policy-making board. What position should the county board take with reference to juvenile delinquency in the county and the education of youth? What position should it take as to what taxes should go for special education or not? Now, another peculiar twist is that the constituent assembly, and by the constituent assembly we say, that this one representative of each school district, whether it be the one representing 201,000 or 100 people, has the ultimate power under the act, this constituent assembly, the ultimate veto power on the amount of taxes that will be levied by this county board. Now, we assert and claim that this is nothing more than a sophisticated method of depriving the people of equal representation, and all the more so in this case because it has the power to tax, because it has the power to bond, because it imposes obligations on people, not school districts, not on stumps, but on everyone. It may have and does have the power to impose the same tax on an elector, a person who lives in the Grand Rapids School District, where there are 201,000 people, as it has for Nelson Center that has 100 people. And we submit that with this all-powerful power to tax, that with this all-powerful policy-making legislative body, which it is, in determining policy in the county of Kent, that it must be under logic, common sense, because it is the contention of the appellant, James Saylor's and others in this case. I didn't quite understand what you said after it has the power to tax. You then said it had the power to do something else. I didn't understand whether it was to borrow or to buy. Which did you say? I said, I'm sure it didn't say borrow. Bond? Bond, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justin, bond the public. Bond. Bond, yes. Bond, yes. Which, of course, is an obligation, and it is a borrowing. That's borrowing a little too. The court properly understood. Yes, borrow. Although the other word, yes. Bond, borrow, certainly. Obligate the people. But bond the whole county. Yes, sir. Now, it is of such importance, and both sides in this case agree, that it is a very important board, that it has very important functions. And we understand, and we content, that any legislative body that has the power to tax, and tax on people, should therefore be one that represents people, or the people should be permitted to vote taxation-wise, or vote on the legislation themselves. Not an old town hall system. But either the people should have the power to vote on taxes, or the power to give direction to the county school board's function, to whether a school should or should not be set up for juvenile delinquents, whether they should or should not have special education to provide for retarded children and otherwise. Either the people should have this direct power to vote on it, or its representatives should have one or the other. One or the other. And that the people of the Grand Rapids School District certainly are deprived of the power to vote equally, because they don't have equal representation. Does it make any difference to you what the actual result in this case was, in terms of where the five-man board came from? Was the election held? It would make no difference to us where they came from, Garner. Would it more than one or one from Grand Rapids? No, it would not, Your Honor, whether they came from Grand Rapids or they all came from Nelson Center. Where did they come from in this case? Mr. Justice White, one of them came from the city of Grand Rapids, as has been stated in the briefs, as a courtesy. They allowed the city of Grand Rapids to have one. The other four came from out county, and traditionally come from out county, that is, other than the city of Grand Rapids. One of them, as a matter of fact, that voted in this case to de-annex certain property from the Grand Rapids School District, had a proposition before the same board, and he moved, or seconded the motion, to de-annex a piece of property from the Grand Rapids School District, and at a subsequent meeting, he, coming from the Grand Rapids School District, one of the smaller ones, was likewise awarded a piece of property from the Grand Rapids School District. That is to say, proposed or seconded the motion to de-annex a piece of territory from the Grand Rapids School District on one occasion, and had pending before the same body at the same time, a petition to de-annex another piece, and he was given. What if the Michigan law provided for appointment of county school boards by the governor? And the governor made the same appointments to this particular county school board, that the same people from the same places. And Grand Rapids would feel like it had been left out, with only one out of five men. Would they have any complaint under Reynolds against them? Yes, Mr. Justice White, I believe they would. It would certainly satisfy part of it, that the responsibility of the governor, that is, being elected by all of the people. As far as the people of the county of Kent, and specifically the city of Grand Rapids School District, is concerned, the governor is accountable to everybody. It would be a vast improvement. But we insist that it would be clearly unconstitutional, because we, as citizens, have the right to participate in the election of those who impose taxes upon us. What if the court disagreed with you on that? The governor could appoint whoever he wanted to, as far as the Constitution was concerned. Would that also determine this case? I could say, very candidly, partially it would, apart from the constitutional aspects of saying that we can't vote for people who spread taxes or levy taxes. On us, at least the members of the Kent County Board would not be accountable to 2 or 5 or 18 percent of the population for their reelection. At least it would be, presumably, an at-large type of representation. I would say, apart from the power to tax and the power to bond, that that would be an appropriate solution, as far as we're concerned. But with the power to tax and bond, with these legislative powers, to lay taxes on the people and levy them, and require everybody to pay them, I would submit, Mr. Justice White, that those rights belong with the people to elect their representatives. Now, we submit that our County Board of Education, or Intermediate School District, as it is now called, is just as much a part of county government as is any other countywide phase of government. We submit it is just as important as this Court has indicated that probably education is the most important thing that government handles on the local level these days. And certainly, from the record, the size of the budgets and the amount of hours and time and participation by the large number of citizens would seem to justify that. We are told that we are told that we should go to the state legislature and ask for a remedy there. But this is a political question. We submit that it is no more a political question as such, or one in which we should have to receive our redress from the legislature, than was the case of Reynolds v. Sims, in which it was recognized. That a great imbalance in representation may be corrected before the courts. And this is the thing which we seek and ask for in this case. How many school districts are there in Kent County, Mr. White? As of today, Mr. Justice Stewart, there are 21 school districts. And does each one of those school districts have the same number of members on its local district school board? No, they do not. They're rated by the size of the school board, whether it is a second-class school district or a third-class school district. But they are properly, independently elected at large. At large by the district. Yes. No trouble there. By the people in the district. By the people in the district. The people in the district. And how many members are there? What does it range from about three to around nine or what is it? Five to nine. Five to nine. And then one of those five to nine goes every two years to a biennial meeting to elect five members of the county school board. That's right, Your Honor. How is that one selected? How is the one representative of each school district? By the county board, not... By the district board. By the district board. Yes, but by the individual school board. It elects one of its members to go. That's right. As a representative of that school district. Yes, sir. And then the election of the five members of the county school board, I realize they're staggered terms, or at least I think I... That's right, two at a time. Two at a time. The fifth one. That membership is elected by the deputies at this biennial meeting. From among their members? From among themselves they elect? No, anyone may be elected. This is an interesting also wrinkle under the act that if a person wants to be elected, he must go to the people and get 50 signatures to be nominated. This is why we call it an election that actually has its antecedents back in the people themselves. He gets 50 signatures nominating petition to become eligible for election by this constituent assembly of the various school district. To election as a member of the county school board. That's right. And he can be a stranger. He can be a non-member of any district school board. He could be legally a non-member. But he usually is a member of one of the district school boards, is he? Whether he's usually or not, it comes to mind there are at least two at this time who are members of school boards. One of them from Grand Rapids by courtesy. One of them I know of the Granville School District, which is one of those districts. Any from Nelson Center? You've been telling us an awful lot about Nelson Center. Not currently, Your Honor. As a matter of fact, I think it has been furnished to this court by my opposition that Nelson Center ceased to exist as a school district just recently. I raise it for this reason, that the board that passed upon the de-annexation that came up in this case was elected. One of the votes being that of Nelson Center, Your Honor. And this is the posture in which this case comes. On the other hand, I'm not at all reluctant to pursue this question or observation the court makes that we still have some 18 to 20 percent that control the whole majority, population-wise. Under the 21 that we now have that can control the whole county board. The county school board has the power to impose taxes. Yes, it does. Up to a certain limitation, I suppose. Well, as long as it's within the 15 mils. And as a practical matter, it never is. But it certainly has the right to impose taxes up to the 15 mils, and it has a right to or not to impose a special half-mil for what we call special education, help the remedial reading retardant. And it has power to make policy decisions, I expect. It has vast powers to make policy decisions. It has vast powers to make policy decisions. I expect the special schools and the track system and various other educational proposals. It has vast powers to empower it to go ahead and make policy decisions. As a matter of fact, one of the annual reports that is within the transcript of record, the county school board superintendent makes the observation. He said, we are the people who should be acting as the intermediary for you local people to the state. He said, meaning and implying quite obviously, that we should be helping you solve the metropolitan problems of this county. We submit, Your Honor, they can't be solved when the people of the Grand Rapids School District can be deprived of all representation on the board. Now, what powers do the local school, the 21 school districts have? What powers do they have within their school districts? Largely to run their own districts. I suppose they have some policy-making functions, don't they? Certainly they do. Certainly they do. Certainly they do. They have large powers. The largest, vast powers within the particular school district as are outlined in legislation in the transcript record, they have a repository of this. Do they have any taxing power within their district? Yes, they do, Your Honor. Within their district? Yes, they do, Your Honor. They have vast taxing power to take care of many of the problems that they have within their individual districts. However, as I have indicated to this court, that additional powers have been, by legislation, or state legislature imposed or given to the county board, which are extremely important, particularly to the Grand Rapids School District in this case, to help meet, we submit, 20th century problems that, in the core city, now occupied by large numbers of culturally deprived people. That this is necessary, that this is necessary, that the Grand Rapids School District should have some sort of proportional representation so that these people who have the power to tax, who have the power to make policy decisions, who have the power, as the superintendent says, to be an appropriate vote policy-wide between the local district and the state district, to properly interpret those things to the state. Now, the school district, the Grand Rapids School District, as you told me, as I understand it, itself has power to impose taxes within its district. Yes, it does. Has power to make policy within its district. Yes, it does. Then can the county school board reverse or veto any of those decisions by the district? It cannot. It cannot. Its powers are supplemental to it. Supplemental to it. They can't take away anything or overrule anything that the Grand Rapids District has decided to do. We do not claim that, and it is not true. It does not have the power to do that. Only possibly... Conflict does not come to mind, Your Honor, and I cannot answer that the county board would prevail in it. Why does the county board have the power to do that? Why does the county board have the power to do that? Why does the county board have the power to do that? Because in the supplemental powers, Your Honor, on the matter of setting up school for delinquents, that's a county board function alone given to the county board. On the matter of special education, this is given to the county board. On the matter of policy representing between the local school districts and the state in developing policy to our state board, this is given to the county board. But if your chairman boardnet says... Ten propagates state anybody board unit communities full increase high bakefulness land collections destruction ruin placingチャージ Mr. Chief Justice, I would say that the policy that would prevail would be the one that was decided by the State Board of Education. It could make the decision of what was to prevail. Specifically, answering your question, I would say that the county board would not necessarily, would not have the power to override the local school district on policy matter as such. When I was addressing, can it? I'm not aware that it can, Your Honor. I am aware that, yes, it has the power to go ahead and build another high school. Yes, it has all those powers, Your Honor, to go right ahead, if it had the money, if it could, if it would, with the problems that it has, with the core city that it has for its tax base of what it may have, whatever it may have, it has those powers. Legally speaking, it has those powers. Thank you, Your Honor. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. The question is whether the composition of local units of government is a state matter and not a subject within the jurisdiction of the court. Or, to put it another way, will the court extend Reynolds into this new and uncharted political thicket? Will the court assume that a constitutionally apportioned legislature will fail to correct any male apportionment in its boards, in its agencies, in its instrumentalities, when corrective measures are needed? In the many briefs, in the briefs, political thicket, a constitutional phrase? It was first used, I believe, by Mr. Justice Freitfurt. I think we either held it wasn't a political thicket. You held that, but this, my point is, is a new thicket and not the one that Mr. Justice Freitfurt was talking about. Is it better or worse? I think so. Actually, I think there are many more brambles in this thicket, Mr. Justice Douglas, than in the one Mr. Justice Freitfurt was talking about. Is it your position that the principle cannot apply to any local government? Is that the position you are taking here? That is my position on behalf representing the Kent County Board of Education. Flat. Well, you don't need to take any such broad position. We don't need to take any such broad position. That's true in representing Kentwood, Your Honor. Exactly. You're talking about one Board of Education in one state with a particular and specific organizational setup. Talking about the Kent County Board of Education and the Kentwood Public Schools, which is hurt by this thing in a financial way. No. Now, I think it is conceded in all of the briefs that have been filed that there is no federal right to vote in local elections. I think that is conceded. Now, I think that also all of the briefs concede that the power of the state to create and abolish local units, government, is absolute. Now, we move to the third. Well, the state could, I assume, abolish its legislature, too, couldn't it? Thank you, pardon me? The people of the state could abolish their legislature, too, couldn't it? Well, I'm not sure that I read the Fortson case that way, Mr. Justice Justice. As I understand the Fortson case, the majority of the court took the position that there is nothing in the federal constitution or its amendments that requires Georgia to elect a governor by popular election. Now, at least that's one step in the direction. As I understand it, in Pakistan, at the local level, everybody votes. They elect one person who goes to a constituent assembly. That person votes the delegation to the next constituent assembly on up to the top. Pakistan is not unique in that respect. No, but I say, could that be done by... I think that the municipal legislature, within its constitution, its constitution, Well, that's something else. I'm talking about a constitution of a state drawn along those lines. Would that be constitutional? I don't know of a constitution that's drawn along that line. Certainly there isn't a constitution. I'm going to ask you if there is one. I said, could one be drawn along those lines? Well, in our democratic form of government with a small d, I think that it might be possible, but I'm not aware that there is any such a constitution of a nation. Now, if that'd be possible, then, what you're talking about is... It would also be possible by a constitutional amendment. Now, what we have, Mr. Justice Douglas, as I understand it, in our country is a republican form of government, which means that the people elect representatives to cast their ballot. Now, that goes through the whole wolf of our entire system of states. Now, that requires, I think, in the broad, in our system of government, in our political philosophy, that requires that in our particular states, without the federal constitution, that we must provide some appropriate method of our interior works. Now, the Constitution of the United States, particularly the second section of the 14th Amendment, does make some specific provisions as to what you have to do in electing both representatives and senators in Congress and what you have to do also within your own state. But with those limitations, I think that a state which is constitutionally apportioned, I think very definitely that a state whose legislature, and the one in Michigan, I think, is one of the best in the country today, after they are properly apportioned, I think that under the Constitution of Michigan, in most states, the legislature has the absolute power to make, create, and abolish agencies for its better government. No matter how inequitable it might be. The question of equity in this phase of it, of the instrumentality of government, is unique. Go back to Hunter v. Pittsburgh. Go back to Attorney General v. Lowry. The people in those cases were overwhelmed and had no right because in these transfers of territory, as has been pointed out, it's an analogy, it's a good analogy, in these transfers of territory, the people have never had a right to vote. Now, in this very case, an odd thing, there were 35 annexations to the city of Grand Rapids. In the context of what we're talking about in the case at Barr, 35 under the Home Rule Act, the school code at that time provided that by reason of such annexations, that territory, as a matter of law, became a part of the Grand Rapids School District. Now, because Kentwood was a new school district, and there had been nine pieces of territory taken away from it without a semblance, without any right whatever to the people of Kentwood to be heard or to vote, after those nine, they went to the legislature and got that section of the statute received. So that today, where there is an annexation under the Home Rule Act, that territory still stays in the school district. Now, what triggered this case, this piece of territory was a part of Kentwood. It was taken away by one of these Home Rule annexations without a vote of the Kentwood school electors. We went back immediately because of the dependencies, as a matter of fact, the legislature had passed a repeal, but it hadn't become effective. We went back to the County Board of Education and asked them not to take it away from the Grand Rapids Board of Education, but to give it back to us. That's what this case is about. Now, there's another thing. My brother cites the 1960 census. One of the reasons that I mention the brambles about this political thicket, in 1960, the figures that my brother cites, Grand Rapids had 55% of the population. In their own brief, they admit that in 1963, it had dropped to 48%. Now, I just... In the brief, in the affidavit, I don't think there's any dispute. As of now, as of now, the 20 school districts, there are 21, including Grand Rapids, the 20 school districts on the periphery of the city of Grand Rapids, have not only a majority of the population, more than 50% of the population, they have over 17,000 more school children according to the 1966 census. The 67 will be taken next month. And not only that, they have more dollars in valuation. So here we are today. They say, give us one man, one vote. We want the County Board of Education to be a portion. I don't know how, because they haven't said it. As I understand, it's done one of two ways possible. We'll elect them at large, or suggest to the legislature they create districts. Okay. Reynolds has applied to our situation. Instead of any relief, to my brother and his client, the Grand Rapids Board of Education, because they've got more voters in the 20 districts, as a matter of politics, they can go out and elect all five. He says that by courtesy, Mrs. Keillor is a member of the board. As a matter of fact, when we started the hearing, I requested that she not sit, because she was wearing two hats. She elected to sit. A few years after that, in 1965, the legislature caught up with it, and provided now that members of county boards can't sit on a transfer proposition, when they are actually members of both boards. Now, you go to a districting proposition. Suppose this court should suggest to the Michigan legislature, or through the Supreme Court of Michigan, that what you should do, Ms. Representative, the type of argument, that what you should do is to create districts. All right? The population is still with the 20 school districts. They've got 17,000 more school children, and they've got more valuation than my brother talks about on tax. So, unless there's political gerrymandering, as I read in the papers, as happened in some of these legislative apportionment things, unless there's gerrymandering, the result would be the same. Mr. Stryker, let's assume that the Michigan law provided for the direct election of the county school board by the people, and that the two parties, or the three parties, or how many have put up candidates for all five positions, and they're all elected every two years, and they're elected by districts. I suppose your position is that Reynolds against Sims wouldn't catch that situation either because it's a local governmental unit. That's correct, Mr. Stryker. Let's assume that you were wrong on that. Assume that I'm wrong, and the result so far is... And assume that Reynolds against Sims would require that those districts for the election of county school board members had to be of equal size population-wise. That's exactly what I was saying, Your Honor, that even whether it's a general election or whether it's by district, in our particular case, the result would be the same, and Reynolds versus Sims would not help at all because no matter how you... No matter how you consider it, there are more voters in the 20 school districts than in Grand Rapids. There are more children. There is more valuation. You would say, then, that if Reynolds against Sims applied to my example of the direct election by districts of the county school board, you would say automatically, then, that Reynolds against Sims has to apply to this situation that you have in this case and that this case has to satisfy Reynolds against Sims? I don't say that. I don't say that. Well, what would keep Reynolds against Sims from applying to this case if it applied to the direct election? Well, Reynolds versus Sims would not answer the problem of my brothers in the city of Grand Rapids in this case at all because one of the assumptions of Reynolds versus Sims is to correct an imbalance in minorities, to help out minorities, to get the minorities an equal weight in vote, with which I agree. And the majority... At the legislative level. But the trouble is that you've still got majorities. And what I'm saying is that here is the odd situation of a minority coming up here and saying, apply Reynolds versus Sims because we want equal votes and you give them equal votes and the majority is still... is with the school districts outside of Grand Rapids and they'll go out and elect at large the five members of the board. They have the political power. Not only that, you create districts. I understand Reynolds versus Sims. The districts must be as near equal population as possible. If that is true and it follows, then the same situation politically applies if it's done honestly and not by gerrymandering because the majority will still be with the 20 school districts on the outside. Michigan, for I'd say at least a hundred years has provided in the general school laws that all local so-called local boards of education be elected at large. Be elected at large. For instance, the Grand Rapids board is a second-class school district with only two in the other city in Flint. And by these statutes regulating second class, they have nine members. Now those nine members of that board are elected at large three at a time every year or so. Three at a time by the entire city of Grand Rapids. Now it is the members of those boards who get together and from their membership select one each two years to go to this other assembly for the purpose of selecting, and I use the word selecting, for the purpose of selecting.
